a00a8ef42f2c5c7a1765e92178bef454.text: B.C. ostrich farm files lawsuit against CFIA, government and RCMP | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. ostrich farm files lawsuit against CFIA, government and RCMP Edgewood's Universal Ostrich Farm has filed a lawsuit against the CFIA, government and RCMP. Almost one year after more than 300 ostriches were killed, the owners are suing. Universal Ostrich Farm and Landco Ventures filed a multi-million dollar civil claim Oct. 30 against the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), Attorney General of Canada and the RCMP. The farm’s representatives Karen Espersen and Katiey Pasitney, say the lawsuit arises from a series of “aggressive and intrusive regulatory actions that culminated in an invasive 52-day occupation of the plaintiffs’ Edgewood, B.C., farm property, the forced slaughter of their ostrich flock, and the destruction of a commercial enterprise.” “As we mark one year since the devastating destruction of our 351 ostriches on Nov. 6–7, 2025, we honour their lives, our family’s 35-year legacy, and the people around the world who continue to stand with us,” said the mother and daughter. “This memorial week, we have filed our civil lawsuit seeking justice, accountability, and meaningful policy change.” They are claiming unlawful search and occupation on or about Sept. 3, 2025 by the CFIA and RCMP, inadequate statutory compensation, animal cruelty and missing birds, unlawful seizure of ostrich eggs, and property damage and trespassing. “This lawsuit is about more than compensation. It is about protecting rights, demanding transparency, and ensuring no other family or animals endure what we experienced.” They are seeking damages for trespass, nuisance, intrusion upon seclusion, and permanent real property devaluation. Relief sought from the court is for an order requiring the defendants to remove all encroachments and remediate the property, a complete accounting and return or compensation for all removed documents, materials, birds, and eggs and general, special, punitive,

6e2009bde2cdc19f5b3c4bb07d88f49a.text: Just as we have expunged any thought of a semi-annual time change, I say it is time to end any notion that sparkling wine has a season. As everyday is a good day for “Bubbles.” Sparkling wine is perfect for a family celebration or an intimate evening. It is ideal alongside popcorn, a charcuterie or Sunday morning brunch. Here is a small selection of B.C. sparkling wines, both Charmat and Traditional Method that will support my belief. A Chardonnay, Pinot Noir blend, Secco is the first Charmat Method sparkling wine from Sandhill. The first and second fermentation in s/s produced a dry, light, fresh bubbly. Copious tiny bubbles carry the apple and citrus aromas and flavours through to the finish. Greet your friends with Secco, soft cheeses and seafood. A Sauvignon Blanc, Gewurztraminer, Viognier blend, with a titch of Pinot Noir and Merlot, Adega Estate Winery’s Espumante is a fun wine. Off-dry, nicely balanced, the pop of the cork greets you with tiny bubbles and an avalanche of fruit on the nose and palate. Enjoy it with your Sunday brunch. An old friend, Ti Amo is a blend of Hester Creek’s estate grown Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat grapes. A wee bit off-dry, after a second stainless steel fermentation, I could happily serve it every day. Aromas and flavours of apple and pear, stone fruits and a smidgeon of spice. Enjoy it alongside a charcuterie of soft cheese and spicy sausage. A Naramata grown blend of Auxerrois, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the 2025 Narrative XC Sparkling wine is delicate, yet it fills your mouth with an explosion of tropical fruit and florals. Concrete, S/S and oak aged, it is fresh and fruit forward. Chill it and enjoy it with Sushi. **Fans of de-alcoholised wine** won’t be disappointed with Narrative XC .05% Sparkling wine. I’d be happy to serve it to my friends or family. A misty rose hue, a crisp and fresh nose and palate of strawberry, oodles of little bubbles lasting to the finish. Serve it with a plate of mild cheese and berries

102aa2c7756af64516c999f790f73b5d.text: A stolen truck collided with a Ford Focus on Sunday, Nov. 1, downtown Quesnel area. Quesnel RCMP are warning the public against taking the law into their own hands after a stolen vehicle was involved in a serious collision Sunday afternoon. According to an RCMP press release, a brown Ford F-250 was reported stolen from a property on Pentland Crescent during the early morning hours of Oct. 30. Mounties said on Nov. 1 that a member of the public spotted the vehicle near the Kersley General Store and pursued it at high speeds into downtown Quesnel. Shortly before 3 p.m., the truck collided with an uninvolved Ford Focus at the intersection of Kinchant Street and Carson Avenue. Although no serious injuries were reported, RCMP said the incident highlights the dangers of members of the public attempting to intervene in criminal matters themselves. “We are reminding the public of the dangers of taking the law into your own hands; thankfully, there were no serious injuries in this collision, but that doesn’t justify the actions of anyone involved,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said. “As a member of the public, there is no way for you to know any previous police or criminal history of the person you are dealing with and the dangers you are exposing yourself or those around you to.” Mounties have identified a man they believe was driving the stolen vehicle and are searching for him after he left the collision scene. According to the release, the individual is known to police. The recovered truck has been seized and towed to a secure location as the investigation continues. Quesnel RCMP are asking anyone who witnessed the incident and has not yet spoken with investigators to come forward. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Quesnel RCMP non-emergency line at 250-992-9211. “Quesnel RCMP would like to thank the witnesses who remained at the scene of the accident to speak with police and aid the victims of the crash,” the release reads.

2c74e06ed4fab09ce3d87435615f92e6.text: Ian Kitchener beside his Atlantic Giant variety pumpkin that will weigh in at 805 lbs. Ian Kitchener's baby giant pumpkin plant early in the growing season. Believe it or not, this single pumpkin plant outgrew its 20 x 24 patch. A family tradition that goes back to 1983: growing the largest pumpkin. Ian Kitchener sits on his 805 lb pumpkin in the back (it's too heavy to move, of course). After a heavy August downpour, the pumpkin took on so much water it got a split. To keep it from rotting, Ian Kitchener put a shelter over top and a fan to dry the wound out. Growing big pumpkins ain't easy. A friend with a crane helps Ian Kitchener lift his giant pumpkin for its weigh in. Anyone who saw Courtenay resident Ian Kitchener’s giant pumpkin would be excused for thinking that Cinderella’s coach was more fact than fairy tale. His colossal squash tips scales at 805 lbs—roughly the weight of four refrigerators—and Kitchener isn’t even a gardener. While it could be assumed that Kitchener was born with a green (or orange) thumb, the truth is that growing an 805 lb pumpkin came from years of trial, error, and toil. “The first couple of attempts weren’t very good. Not knowing anything, I just dug up all the topsoil and planted it in dirt, and it didn’t work. So I stopped for a year or two, then got at it again, did it a little better, then a little better… It became a little like an obsession.” This little obsession has roots that stretch back to 1983, when the Kitcheners, a local family with agricultural kin, started the annual tradition of who could grow the largest pumpkin. Ian Kitchener’s grandfather participated in that first friendly competition with a pumpkin that weighed around 30 lbs. The tradition has carried on through the generations, and now the cousins are competing. In addition to bragging rights, the winner’s name and the pumpkin’s weight are etched onto a plaque for posterity, and last place has to host next year’s weigh-in and goes home with a boob mug. Last

Ekene Anigbo has been ordered to serve 15 years less time served for the death of a Naramata woman. Anigbo appeared in B.C. Supreme Court in Kelowna the morning of Monday, Nov. 2 for sentencing after he was found guilty of manslaughter for the 2021 death of 57-year-old Kathleen Richardson. The 27-year-old stood trial for first-degree murder, but was convicted on Aug. 14 of the lesser charge of manslaughter after a lengthy trial that began in March. Justice Alison Beames found the Crown had not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Anigbo had fired the shots that killed 57-year-old Richardson inside her home. However, the Crown proved that Anigbo and co-accused Jalen Falk worked together, entering the residence to search for Richardson’s son, Wade Cudmore, in the early morning of June 9, 2021. Richardson was found dead in the basement of her home later that same day. Crown presented during trial that Richardson’s death was part of a larger conspiracy. The conspiracy, Crown presented, started with the death of brothers Erick and Carlos Fryer. Associates of Anigbo believed Cudmore was one of two people involved in the death of the brothers, and that he had stolen drugs and money during the attack. Anigbo and Falk had been tasked to locate Cudmore in order to retrieve the stolen items. Anigbo and Falk had gone to Richardson’s property with at least two guns in their possession. The court heard that the two men attempted to get information about Cudmore from Richardson when it was discovered he was not at the home, however, she fought back as evident from non-fatal injuries sustained to her hands and arms. It was found that Anigbo and Falk worked together to kill Richardson before fleeing the scene. bdd0a199193529a8fd674f4e2ce8e86c.text: Conservative leader and premier designate Lorne Doerkson addresses the new caucus on Monday, Nov. 2. B.C.’s new premier designate, Lorne Doerkson, said the B.C. Conservatives are united when he took the stage on Monday to speak to B.C. residents and his fellow MLAs. On Nov. 2, the first meeting of the majority Conservative caucus was held in Victoria following a landslide victory in the 2026 provincial election. The win was preceded by a turbulent time for the party, rife with floor-crossing, senior staff resignations, allegedly leaked back-door conversations and the resignation of then-leader Kerry Lynn-Findlay. “I know that there will be a lot of commentary about this caucus, and a lot of people watching to see whether or not we can vote together,” he told the crowd of MLAs at the Victoria Marriott. “So let me save everyone the suspense. This caucus is unified.” Under former Tory leader John Rustad, rifts began between more hardline social Conservatives like Tara Armstrong and Dallas Brodie – who was ousted from the party in 2025 – and moderates like Elenore Sturko, who went on to cross to other parties, created parties of their own, and publicly spoke out against party leadership, leading more than a dozen MLAs to resign or leave the party under Findlay’s leadership. “I want all British Columbians to hear this too. [The election] is over. Governing is our focus now, and governing is a different job. Every one of you ran as a Conservative, and every one of you won as a Conservative. But as of today, you represent every single person in this province and in your riding. The people who voted for us, of course, the people who voted against us, and the people who didn’t vote at all, we represent everyone,” he told the crowd. He said people don’t expect perfection from government, but they do expect honesty. To him, that means “saying no to new taxes,” giving PST exemptions for small businesses, returning housing decisions to individual communities and repealing DRIPA

27bec24bcb813f512b0bd9c989e65d94.text: The Coldsnap Festival is coming back to Prince George between Feb. 3 to 7, 2027. Prince George’s Coldsnap festival will celebrate its 20th anniversary with five days of live music next spring. In a press release, the Prince George Folkfest Society announced the mainstage lineup for Coldsnap 2027, bringing together returning favourites and new artists for the milestone winter festival. The festival opens Wednesday, Feb. 3, at Knox Performance Centre with Absolute Legends, featuring performances by Raghu Lokanathan, The Pairs and Juno Award winners The Bros. Landreth. The festival will close on Sunday, Feb. 7, with Bring it Home!, a showcase of B.C.-based artists. According to the society, the finale will feature ellescriv, Desireé Dawson and Alex Cuba, a multiple Juno, Grammy and Latin Grammy Award winner. Other returning performances include Andrea Beaton and Troy MacGillivray, Cécile Doo-Kingué and Diyet. According to the release, Coldsnap will also bring back its family-friendly Coldsnap for Kids event at the Prince George Playhouse on the morning of Feb. 7. This year’s performance will feature the music of Oh Clementine. For late-night audiences, Late Nights at the Legion will return Thursday, Friday and Saturday. A special Late Late Night performance, Midnight Melodies with Elisa Thorn, is scheduled for the early hours following Saturday night’s Legion events. The society added that the festival’s free daytime IceJam and Workshop series will also return at various venues throughout downtown Prince George. Further details about the events are expected in the New Year. Tickets go on sale through the festival website Friday, Nov. 6. Festival passes, available in limited quantities, include admission to all mainstage concerts at Knox Performance Centre and Heritage Hall, as well as Late Nights at the Royal Canadian Legion. b2bffe8fb72533e9e3fa7d10d60a6278.text: TABLES TALES: Painting like a professional? | 100 Mile Free Press A rack of Warhammer Tone Pro paints on display at Creative Magic Art and Hobby. One thing my paint collection never seems to do is grow smaller. Sure, over the years, a few of my paints have either run out or turned into rubber from prolonged exposure to the air, but I never fail to replace them. If anything, when I do, I buy one or two other paints, just to try them out and so the collection grows. I primarily use the acrylic model paints produced by Games Workshop, known as Citadel Paints. While the line has recently been rebranded to Warhammer Paints, the paint’s names, recipe and colours are largely unchanged. Recently, however, a truly new line of paints was announced and launched by Games Workshop: Warhammer Tone Pro. It’s supposed to, as the name suggests, help you paint like a professional. This new line includes only 30 colours, but five different tones of each, numbered with one being the darkest and five being the lightest. The idea is that three for each colour will be used as the base paint, while the darker tones will be used for shading and the lighter tones for highlights. Online, there has been much discourse around these paints, with some praising the fast coverage they provide and how the paint ‘evens out’ naturally. Some have claimed you can simply gloop the paint on thickly and the paint will automatically run and dry in a way that preserves the details of the model. Earlier this month, I got a chance to try out a sample of these new paints at Creative Magic Art and Hobby. I was eager to see if these new professional paints were truly worth the hype. I brought along a spare Landsknecht Ogre model I bought off Wargames Atlantic several years ago but never painted beyond a quick prime. I figured a large model like this would allow me to test the coverage of this paint. Overall, I will say I was impressed by the paint’s performance. True to all the hype, the paint spread quickly

Kristin Buxton (left), Rick McKinney and Kim Fraser are all members of the Canadian Mental Health Association staff who help run the new Soups On! program. Leslie Silveria enjoys a cup of soup at the Canadian Mental Health Association on Friday, October 30. Alexis Stone enjoys a cup of soup at the Canadian Mental Health Association on Friday, October 30. It’s a simple activity on its face, yet it’s one that has created countless connections across the millennia. That age-old tradition has been carried on at the Canadian Mental Health Association South Cariboo Branch with its new weekly Soups On! Free Friday Soup Program. The program has been running every Friday since mid-September from 10:30 to 11:30 a.m. Homeless outreach coordinator Rick McKinney said he wants to see the program expand and invites the entire community to enjoy a bowl of hot soup together. “It’s been great. Our first couple, we had five people and we have had up to nine people eat in and have soup with us. Everyone who comes in usually gets a to-go soup and everything else goes out to do outreach in the community,” McKinney said. “A couple of the seniors who were coming every week have spoken about how it’s making them feel less lonely, less isolated and they look forward to coming every week. We’re hopeful we’ll get more people and steam will start to pick up.” McKinney said about two years ago, when he took on the role, he thought it would be nice to try something a little different. He explained that while working at a homeless shelter in Squamish, he saw firsthand how people connected over food. In 100 Mile House, McKinney said he noticed a lack of those kinds of resources and wanted to help address it. dbf048cfbca0199e4255f28377908e66.text: The Williams Lake Fire Department responded to four dumpster fires in different areas of the city on Monday, Nov. 2. The City of Williams Lake is encouraging residents to remain vigilant after a series of dumpster fires broke out in a relatively short period of time. According to a Monday, Nov. 2 Facebook post the Williams Lake Fire Department responded to four small dumpster fires in different areas of the city over a period of approximately 45 minutes. “Crews responded quickly to each incident and were able to extinguish the fires before they spread,” the post read. “There were no injuries and no damage to surrounding property.” The city stated while there is currently no indication of a broader threat to public safety, residents are encouraged to remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity, smoke or fire concerns. Residents and businesses are also reminded to keep dumpsters clear of surrounding debris and combustible materials and, where possible, ensure dumpster lids and enclosures remain secured. “Thank you for looking out for one another and helping keep Williams Lake safe,” Mayor Surinderpal Rathor additionally wrote on Facebook.

c8a806c277fe7306695d904fc39baa28.text: A grizzly bear, like the one pictured here, is suspected to be behind the death of a hiker near Bella Coola. The BC Conservation Officer Service is investigating a suspected fatal bear attack near Bella Coola. The second victim of a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola has been located dead. The BC Conservation Officer Service said in a post on social media that the second victim was located this afternoon during search efforts by conservation officers and the RCMP. “Throughout the day, our priorities were to secure the area and protect officers and first responders as they searched for the missing person, then respectfully recover the deceased so they could be brought home to their family,” the post reads. “We extend our deepest condolences to both families. We remain committed to supporting them as our investigation continues.” BCCOS noted that officers continue to work to locate and capture any bears involved in the incident and added that it isn’t clear whether more than one bear was involved in the incident. The government agency said that any bears captured will be assessed to determine the appropriate next steps. If a bear is determined to be responsible for the attack, it will be dispatched to ensure public safety, in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines. “Search efforts have concluded. We continue to urge people to stay away from the Snooka West Trail area for their own safety and to give officers the space and time needed to do this work,” the post reads. BCCOS added they remain in regular contact with the Nuxalk Nation, members of the community and law enforcement as well as emergency response partners. The government agency added that further updates are expected as the investigation continues. One person has been found dead following a suspected grizzly bear attack near Bella Coola, as search efforts continue for a second missing individual. 44620c28a5616a16f4e04111067e69bf.text: The Union of B.C. Municipalities had to appoint a new president following the Oct. 17 municipal elections. Following her unsuccessful mayoral bid, Squamish Coun. Jenna Stoner has been replaced as Union of B.C. Municipalities president just one month after taking the position. Per UBCM bylaws, first vice-president Sarrah Storey replaced Stoner. Incumbents fared poorly in municipal races across the province in the Oct. 17 local elections, and change on town and city councils also means change in umbrella organizations made up of local officials. “It’s a hard thing when we lose really great elected officials, and we lost a lot this year,” Storey said. Stoner was elected by acclamation in September at the UBCM conference in mid-September, and her term as president lasted only about one month. UBCM officials say they cannot find another instance of a president being forced out by losing a re-election bid. “I’m disappointed that I won’t be back around the table,” Stoner said. “The work that the organization does is very important and vital to all local government across the province. It was a real honour to be able to serve even a short term as president for that organization.” Stoner knew that running for mayor in Squamish risked her job as UBCM president, a role she was elevated to as a councillor. She ultimately lost the mayoral contest to Sean Easton by fewer than 200 votes. Six out of seven council seats in Squamish also turned over on Oct. 17, reflecting a wider provincewide trend of incumbents losing. Second vice-president Aimee Grice is out at UBCM as well, after losing her bid to move from council to the mayor’s office in Oliver. Despite the leadership changes, members set UBCM’s policy direction at a convention, and it should remain the same under Storey’s presidency. “My goal is to make sure that I am working on behalf of the priorities of our members, and those priorities obviously come from our resolutions and things that the members have identified,” Storey

Next summer’s FVDED in the Park dance music festival will grow to three days at Holland Park in Surrey. While no DJs are announced yet, the festival website shows 2027 dates of July 9, 10 and 11. FVDED has always been a two-day dance party in Surrey over the past decade-plus. “A 15-year milestone deserves main-character energy,” fest organizers post on social media Nov. 2. “FVDED is bringing 3 days, 4 stages and over 75+ international artists to Holland Park. Time to go big.” Festival “super early bird” tickets are sold on fvdedinthepark.com starting Tuesday, Nov. 10. Last July, an event-record 54,000 dance music fans showed up for the 2026 FVDED in the Park, featuring headliners Dom Dolla, Fisher, Griz and many others. Could the 2027 festival hit 80,000 attendance over three days? 13ad3b5d3f70c340368dc6b5232d05ba.text: Joseph Camilleri, 76, completed the Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Challenge after crossing the finish line at the Berlin Marathon on Sept. 27. Victoria's Joseph Camilleri, known in the running community as "Crazy Legs," completed his sixth major marathon in Berlin, finishing the race in 4:51:25. Joseph Camilleri has run thousands of kilometres to reach the finish line. At 76, he finally has all six medals to show for it. The Victoria runner completed the Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Challenge on Sept. 27, crossing the finish line at the Berlin Marathon in 4:51:25 to complete a journey that began in Boston in 2018. The challenge requires runners to complete six of the world’s major marathons: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago and New York City. Born in Malta, Camilleri first moved to England, then came to Canada in 1972 at 22 years old, joining his brother in Winnipeg. He later moved to Toronto before landing in Victoria in 2010. He said his research suggests he is the oldest Maltese-Canadian athlete to complete the challenge, a distinction that makes the accomplishment even more special. Known around Victoria’s running community as “Crazy Legs,” Camilleri’s final marathon came after a difficult year of injuries, setbacks and uncertainty about whether he would make it to the starting line. 71f6c78a417878011949341b261d8516.text: A growing memorial for the victims in the Lapu Lapu Day festival attack sits at the corner of East 41st Avenue and Fraser Street. Friday, May 2 was a provincial day of mournlng and remembrance for the attack that killed 11 and injured at least two dozen others on April 26, 2025. Adam Kai-Ji Lo, the accused in the fatal car ramming at the 2025 Lapu Lapu event in Vancouver, has pleaded not guilty to all charges. The B.C. Prosecution Service confirmed to Today In BC that Lo pleaded not guilty to the 11 second-degree murder charges and the additional 31 attempted murder charges in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver on Monday (Nov. 2). Lo is in the midst of a 22-day voir dire, a mini hearing to determine whether evidence can be admitted at trial. A provincial court judge, Reginald Harris, found him mentally fit to stand trial on Sept. 10, 2025. The trial was moved to B.C. Supreme Court earlier this year. He is expected to stand trial beginning April 19, 2027, at the Vancouver Law Courts. The trial is expected to continue for four months. The B.C. Prosecution Service says pretrial applications are currently underway and are expected to continue until mid-March 2027. Lo is accused of driving an SUV into a crowd of people at the Lapu Lapu Day block party in Vancouver on April 26, 2025. He was arrested at the scene. Eleven people were killed – seven women, two men, one non-binary person and a five-year-old girl – and at least two dozen more were injured, ranging in age from 22 months old to 60 years old. Initially charged with eight counts of second-degree murder the day after the incident, another three second-degree murder charges were approved by the prosecution service on July 22, 2025. b41aed452321c14d9914d1c1bdbec00e.text: A stolen truck collided with a Ford Focus on Sunday, Nov. 1, downtown Quesnel area. Quesnel RCMP are warning the public against taking the law into their own hands after a stolen vehicle was involved in a serious collision Sunday afternoon. According to an RCMP press release, a brown Ford F-250 was reported stolen from a property on Pentland Crescent during the early morning hours of Oct. 30. Mounties said on Nov. 1 that a member of the public spotted the vehicle near the Kersley General Store. A second witness spotted the vehicle near Highway 97 and Racing Road and pursued it at high speeds into downtown Quesnel. Shortly before 3 p.m., the truck collided with an uninvolved Ford Focus at the intersection of Kinchant Street and Carson Avenue. Although no serious injuries were reported, RCMP said the incident highlights the dangers of members of the public attempting to intervene in criminal matters themselves. “We are reminding the public of the dangers of taking the law into your own hands; thankfully, there were no serious injuries in this collision, but that doesn’t justify the actions of anyone involved,” Cpl. Jennifer Cooper, BC RCMP spokesperson for Northern B.C., said. “As a member of the public, there is no way for you to know any previous police or criminal history of the person you are dealing with and the dangers you are exposing yourself or those around you to.” Mounties have identified a man they believe was driving the stolen vehicle and are searching for him after he left the collision scene. According to the release, the individual is known to police. The recovered truck has been seized and towed to a secure location as the investigation continues. Quesnel RCMP are asking anyone who witnessed the incident and has not yet spoken with investigators to come forward.
